en.question: Which visible feature in this knee crop supports meniscal chondrocalcinosis?

options.text: Fine linear calcification in the meniscal joint-space region.
Subchondral sclerosis at the weight-bearing articular surfaces.
Marginal bony spurs at the joint contour.
Narrowing of the femorotibial joint space.

en.explanation: Fine linear densities in the meniscal region support the imaging finding of chondrocalcinosis. Sclerosis, osteophytes or joint-space narrowing may coexist, but are not the calcification sign asked for. This finding alone does not establish an acute CPPD flare.

wrongExplanations.B: Subchondral sclerosis lies in bone beneath cartilage, not as a fine meniscal line.
wrongExplanations.C: Osteophytes are marginal bony spurs, distinct from meniscal calcific lines.
wrongExplanations.D: Joint-space width is a separate finding and does not itself demonstrate meniscal calcification.

image.alt: Magnified femorotibial joint-space crop from a knee radiograph.
image.caption: Existing source crop from MSK.pdf, PDF p.56 / printed p.55.

sources: MSK.pdf physicalp56; actual stored joint-detail image inspected2026-10-25

en.question: Radiographs show meniscal calcification. MRI shows increased meniscal PD signal without definite surface contact or a morphological defect. Which approach is best justified?

options.text: Assign the signal to a degenerative horizontal tear, giving surface and shape signs less weight.
Treat the signal as an activity marker and assign an acute CPPD flare.
Correlate radiographs and assess independent surface/shape signs before assigning a tear.
Attribute the signal to calcification and stop looking for a coexisting meniscal lesion.

en.explanation: Chondrocalcinosis can appear bright and mimic a tear, while a true tear may coexist. Assess the radiographic pattern, adjacent slices, definite surface contact and morphology together. The cause of current symptoms requires clinical context.

wrongExplanations.A: High PD signal alone is not reliable evidence of a tear in chondrocalcinosis.
wrongExplanations.B: Deposition and signal do not establish a current inflammatory attack.
wrongExplanations.D: Calcification provides a possible source of signal but does not exclude a coexisting tear.

en.question: An active adolescent has activity-related tenderness over the tibial tuberosity. The distal patellar tendon attachment is thickened and reactive at that site. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.text: Sinding–Larsen–Johansson syndrome at the inferior patellar pole.
Osgood–Schlatter lesion at the tibial tuberosity.
Proximal patellar tendinopathy at the inferior patellar pole.
Irritation of a bipartite patella at the superolateral fragment.

en.explanation: The tibial-tuberosity and distal patellar-tendon location fits an Osgood–Schlatter lesion. Assess symptoms, tendon and surrounding soft tissues together; fragmentation alone is insufficient.

wrongExplanations.A: This alternative is at the inferior patellar pole, not the tibial tendon attachment.
wrongExplanations.C: Proximal patellar tendinopathy affects the patellar attachment, not the described tibial attachment.
wrongExplanations.D: A superolateral patellar fragment is a different anatomical location.

sources: Existing patella/extensor and Osgood lessons: distal versus proximal insertion localisation

en.question: An adult German-language report uses “Osteochondrosis intervertebralis” for degenerative disc and adjacent osseous changes. Which meaning fits this context?

options.text: Acute traumatic growth-cartilage injury.
Childhood osteonecrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis.
German-language terminology for adult degenerative disc changes.
Growth disturbance of vertebral endplates as in Scheuermann disease.

en.explanation: The source describes German-language use for adult disc degeneration with an osseous reaction, giving degenerative disc disease as the English term. Age, location and the full report prevent confusion with childhood osteochondroses.

wrongExplanations.A: An acute physeal injury is traumatic and is explicitly distinguished in the source.
wrongExplanations.B: That description concerns the childhood femoral head, not adult degenerative disc findings.
wrongExplanations.D: Scheuermann concerns growth-related endplate disturbance; the given adult degenerative context differs.

en.question: After a fall, a child has an acute fracture line through the physis. Which classification keeps the source terminology distinct?

options.text: Osteochondrosis solely because the lesion is in growth cartilage.
Acute physeal injury, distinct from the osteochondrosis umbrella term.
Osteochondrosis intervertebralis in the degenerative sense.
Growth disturbance of vertebral endplates (Scheuermann disease).

en.explanation: Location at growth cartilage does not turn an acute traumatic fracture into osteochondrosis. The source distinguishes acute physeal injuries from the group with disturbed endochondral ossification. Describe the specific fracture course separately.

wrongExplanations.A: The acute traumatic fracture course matters here, not location alone.
wrongExplanations.C: The degenerative disc term describes neither a childhood physis nor this acute fracture.
wrongExplanations.D: Scheuermann concerns spinal endplate growth; an acute physeal fracture line belongs to a different category.

en.question: A 12-year-old with open physes has femoral condylar OCD. The fragment is not displaced; MRI shows a high-T2 interface rim. Which assessment of this single sign is appropriate?

options.text: The rim raises concern for instability but alone lacks specificity in juvenile lesions; integrate other findings and clinical course.
The rim characterizes a stable fragment with completed bony healing.
The rim suffices to classify instability using the same interpretation as in adults.
The rim represents a normal ossification variant rather than OCD.

en.explanation: In the arthroscopy-correlated primary study, conventional MRI instability criteria were less specific in juvenile than adult lesions. An interface rim alone therefore cannot establish stability status here. Integrate skeletal maturity, cartilage/subchondral plate, other signs and clinical course.

wrongExplanations.B: A high-T2 rim does not establish completed bony healing.
wrongExplanations.C: Lower specificity in juvenile OCD limits direct transfer of adult criteria.
wrongExplanations.D: An interface rim does not turn the described OCD into a normal ossification variant; assess the distribution and accompanying findings separately.

en.question: In HIV with gradually progressive cognitive slowing, MRI shows relatively symmetric deep/periventricular FLAIR change and diffuse atrophy without an expansile lesion. Which pattern fits best?

options.text: HIV-associated encephalopathy
Cerebral toxoplasmosis
Primary CNS lymphoma
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

en.explanation: Symmetric deep white-matter change with volume loss may fit HIV-associated encephalopathy. It is nonspecific; assess other infectious, vascular, and metabolic causes and clinical function.

wrongExplanations.B: Toxoplasmosis more often produces focal, frequently ring-enhancing lesions with oedema; none is described.
wrongExplanations.C: No solid expansile lesion is described; lymphoma cannot be inferred from diffuse atrophy alone.
wrongExplanations.D: PML remains a differential but is classically more focal/asymmetric than the described diffuse pattern.

en.question: In advanced HIV, focal deficits progress over weeks. MRI shows asymmetric subcortical FLAIR lesions involving U-fibres, with little mass effect and enhancement. Which cause should be specifically evaluated?

options.text: Diffuse HIV-associated encephalopathy
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
Cerebral toxoplasmosis
Primary CNS lymphoma

en.explanation: The subacute progressive focal course and asymmetric white-matter pattern raise concern for PML. CSF JCV PCR can support diagnosis in context; a negative result does not reliably exclude it.

wrongExplanations.A: Focal progression with asymmetric subcortical involvement fits PML better than the typical diffuse HIV pattern.
wrongExplanations.C: Toxoplasmosis typically forms focal lesions with more oedema/mass effect and enhancement than described here.
wrongExplanations.D: Lymphoma more often produces an expansile, frequently enhancing lesion; the nonexpansile subcortical pattern here favours PML.

en.question: With known PML, new clinical deterioration, enhancement, and oedema develop at established lesions after effective ART begins. Which explanation must be prioritised?

options.text: Non-inflammatory progression of classic PML
Diffuse HIV encephalopathy
PML-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (PML-IRIS)
Concurrent cerebral toxoplasmosis

en.explanation: PML-IRIS can occur after ART with inflammatory enhancement, oedema, and mass effect. Timing and established PML are essential; interpretation remains clinical and does not exclude concurrent disease.

wrongExplanations.A: New inflammatory features after effective ART require assessment for IRIS rather than a purely non-inflammatory explanation.
wrongExplanations.B: Diffuse HIV encephalopathy poorly explains inflammatory change at known PML lesions.
wrongExplanations.D: Concurrent infection remains possible, but new inflammation at known PML lesions after immune reconstitution fits PML-IRIS more directly.

en.question: An adult with fever and confusion has thin sulcal enhancement and additional intraparenchymal temporal FLAIR lesions. Which description captures both compartments?

options.text: Meningeal and parenchymal involvement
Isolated meningeal involvement
Isolated parenchymal involvement
Exclusively pachymeningeal dural involvement

en.explanation: Sulcal enhancement involves the leptomeningeal space; the explicitly intraparenchymal lesions lie in brain tissue. This is anatomical pattern description, not proof of infection or a particular pathogen.

wrongExplanations.B: This description omits the temporal parenchymal lesions.
wrongExplanations.C: The additional sulcal enhancement also belongs in the report.
wrongExplanations.D: Sulcal enhancement follows the leptomeninges; parenchymal lesions are also described.

en.question: An adult with fever and meningism has unremarkable FLAIR and contrast-enhanced T1 images. Which conclusion is appropriate?

options.text: A bacterial cause is excluded while a viral cause remains possible
A viral cause is excluded while a bacterial cause remains possible
No corresponding MRI signs; meningitis still requires clinical and CSF assessment
The symptoms can therefore be classified as non-inflammatory

en.explanation: The small original study included normal MRI in viral and bacterial meningitis. Normal MRI neither excludes the disease nor determines its cause; clinical and CSF findings remain essential.

wrongExplanations.A: Bacterial meningitis can also occur without these MRI signs.
wrongExplanations.B: Viral meningitis can also occur with unremarkable MRI.
wrongExplanations.D: Absent MRI signs do not establish a non-inflammatory cause.

en.question: With bacterial meningitis and clinical deterioration, MRI shows new irregular dependent material in the occipital horns, ependymal enhancement and increasing ventricular size. Which complication is particularly concerning?

options.text: Communicating hydrocephalus without intraventricular inflammation
Pyogenic ventriculitis with accompanying hydrocephalus
Subependymal tumour spread
Ex-vacuo enlargement in chronic brain atrophy

en.explanation: Irregular ventricular debris is suspicious for ventriculitis in the appropriate infectious context. Ependymal enhancement and hydrocephalus may accompany it. Assess the material and alternatives including blood products across the examination and communicate concern promptly.

wrongExplanations.A: Enlargement alone does not adequately explain the new debris and ependymal enhancement.
wrongExplanations.C: Tumour can cause ependymal findings, but acute infection and dependent debris here favour an infectious complication.
wrongExplanations.D: Atrophy explains neither new debris nor enhancement suspicious for inflammation.

en.question: An adult develops cognitive decline and myoclonus over weeks. MRI shows multifocal cortical ribboning and caudate signal, more conspicuous on DWI than FLAIR, with corresponding low ADC and no vascular territory. Which diagnosis should be prioritised for evaluation?

options.text: Sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
Hypoxic–ischaemic brain injury
Autoimmune encephalitis
Peri-ictal signal changes

en.explanation: Rapid progression and nonterritorial cortical-striatal restriction raise concern for CJD. MRI is one diagnostic component; clinical assessment, further testing and treatable alternatives remain essential.

wrongExplanations.B: Hypoxia can cause cortical–striatal restriction. Without a reported hypoxic event, progressive decline over weeks with myoclonus prioritises CJD evaluation here.
wrongExplanations.C: Autoimmune encephalitis remains a treatable differential. DWI-predominant cortical–striatal change with low ADC and rapid decline more strongly supports CJD suspicion here; continue clinical evaluation.
wrongExplanations.D: Seizures can mimic cortical diffusion changes. Progressive decline over weeks with multifocal cortical–striatal involvement prioritises CJD evaluation here; seizure history and EEG remain relevant.

en.question: Sporadic CJD is considered in rapidly progressive dementia. Which MRI pattern should particularly prompt evaluation of limbic inflammatory or peri-ictal alternatives?

options.text: DWI-predominant caudate and putamen hyperintensity with corresponding low ADC
Parietal and occipital cortical ribboning with low ADC
Isolated mesial temporal FLAIR predominance without reduced ADC
Multifocal cortical and striatal DWI predominance with ADC reduction

en.explanation: Isolated limbic FLAIR predominance without ADC reduction requires consideration of other causes, including autoimmune or infectious encephalitis and seizure effects. Imaging alone does not reliably separate these; bright DWI is not automatically restriction.

wrongExplanations.A: Striatal DWI predominance with low ADC can support a CJD-suspicious pattern; it is not the isolated limbic FLAIR finding asked for.
wrongExplanations.B: Multiregional neocortical restriction may raise concern for CJD in context. The question asks for the differing isolated limbic pattern.
wrongExplanations.D: Combined cortical and striatal restriction can support CJD but does not prove it. It differs from the isolated limbic comparison pattern.

en.question: During a prion workup, a classic pulvinar sign is described on FLAIR. Which signal comparison belongs to the definition of this sign particularly associated with vCJD?

options.text: Bilateral pulvinar brighter than the anterior putamen
Pulvinar brighter than the caudate as the defining reference
Pulvinar brighter than the remaining thalamus alone
Caudate brighter than the pulvinar

en.explanation: Bilateral pulvinar comparison with the anterior putamen defines the classic sign more precisely. Pulvinar brightness relative only to other thalamic nuclei is not equivalent. Interpret it in the clinical vCJD context rather than as a general sCJD hallmark.

wrongExplanations.B: The caudate is not the defining reference; the classic definition compares bilateral pulvinar with anterior putamen.
wrongExplanations.C: This may describe conspicuous thalamic signal but does not meet the more precise comparison with anterior putamen.
wrongExplanations.D: This reverses the relationship and uses caudate rather than anterior putamen as reference.

en.question: In established femoral-head osteonecrosis, CT shows a subchondral fracture with 3 mm depression. Joint space is preserved, without osteoarthritis. Which 2019 revised ARCO stage fits?

options.text: II
IIIA
IIIB
IV

en.explanation: ARCO 2019 assigns subchondral or necrotic-zone fracture to stage III: IIIA for depression ≤2 mm and IIIB for >2 mm. Stage IV requires radiographic osteoarthritis; depression alone does not make stage IV.

wrongExplanations.A: Stage II has no subchondral/necrotic-zone fracture or flattening; the described structural findings exceed it.
wrongExplanations.B: IIIA applies to depression ≤2 mm. The specified 3 mm exceeds that boundary.
wrongExplanations.D: Preserved joint space without osteoarthritis does not meet the stage-IV setting described here.

en.question: Which bone pattern predominates in the displayed hand radiograph?

options.text: A circumscribed round medullary sclerotic island.
Multiple ring-and-arc matrix calcifications.
Irregular longitudinal cortical hyperostosis.
Diffuse reduced bone density without focal sclerosis.

en.explanation: The image shows longitudinal dense cortical bone overgrowth. In the source case, this pattern supports melorheostosis. Describe visible morphology; a single crop does not establish total extent or soft-tissue involvement.

wrongExplanations.A: The visible dense abnormality follows the cortex longitudinally rather than forming a solitary round medullary island.
wrongExplanations.B: Ring-and-arc calcifications are not the predominant pattern here; the finding is compact cortical bone overgrowth.
wrongExplanations.D: The key finding is locally dense cortex rather than generalized reduced density alone.

image.caption: Source image without added overlays.
image.credit: Radiopaedia rID199384 · image from the user-provided PDF; no contributor named on the source page.
